## SCORE in brief {#score-in-brief .smaller}

::: {.fs-80}
| Repetition | The study | What came back |
|:-----|:-----|:-----|
| **Reproduction** – same data, same analysis | 600 papers from 62 journals, 2009–2018 [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial] | Of the 143 that could be assessed, **53.6%** reproduced precisely and **73.5%** at least approximately; counting the papers that nobody could check, about **18%** |
| **Robustness** – same data, other analyses | Multi100: 100 studies, at least 5 analysts each [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness] | **74%** of reanalyses reached the same conclusion; **34%** came within ±0.05 *d* of the original effect size |
| **Replication** – new data | 274 claims, independent data [@TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial] | **55.1%** significant again; the median effect size fell from *r* = 0.25 to 0.10 |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Measured on the same body of papers, the three are **essentially uncorrelated**: knowing how a finding fared on one tells you almost nothing about the others.
:::

::: notes
SCORE, a programme funded by the research agency of the US Department of Defense, took a sample of social-science papers and put their central claims through each of the three repetitions on the grid. Reproduction first: of six hundred papers, the authors supplied data for about a quarter, and of the hundred and forty-three that could be assessed, about half reproduced precisely and three quarters approximately. Count the papers that nobody could check, and the rate is about eighteen per cent. Robustness was Multi100, where at least five analysts reanalysed each claim: three quarters reached the same conclusion, but only a third came close to the original effect size. Replication on new data: fifty-five per cent significant again, with effect sizes more than halved. [advance] And the three barely predict one another, so for any one paper you have to ask which of the three it passed.
:::
